text:
The paper was brittle, foxed at the edges like old skin. I held it under the lamp’s halo, afraid my breath might turn it to dust. The ink had faded to a bruised purple, but the loops of the *g* and the sharp crossbar of the *t* were unmistakable. It was his hand.

Forty years dead, yet here he was, instructing me on how to fold dumplings. *“Pinch gently,”* the script read, *“as if sealing a secret.”* My thumb traced the groove where the pen had pressed hardest into the page. He had died in a hospital bed, surrounded by sterile sheets and beeping monitors, far from this kitchen. Yet, somehow, he had slipped away during a Tuesday afternoon nap to leave this card tucked inside the family bible.

I looked up from the recipe. The steam from the boiling water curled against the windowpane, blurring the garden outside. For a moment, the scent of ginger and scallions wasn’t just food; it was time travel. A resurrection in three ingredients. I picked up a wrapper, trembling not from age, but from the sudden, heavy weight of being remembered by someone who no longer existed.
